Bitcoin Puzzle Hunter

A fresh, from-scratch Bitcoin puzzle scanner built by Zunid + Muse, running 24/7 on our own VM. It is a lottery, not a brute-forcer — puzzle #71 alone has 270 keys, so no hunter can systematically crack it. It buys lottery tickets with spare CPU.

Speed ~638,000 keys/sec CPU 1 core Targets 78 unsolved puzzles Prize 916.5 BTC

Puzzle #71

7.1 BTC

~51% of scan time · smallest unsolved range

1PWo3JeB9jrGwfHDNpdGK54CRas7fsVzXU — balance re-confirmed live via bitaps, Nov 18, 2026.

Puzzle #72

7.2 BTC

~26% of scan time

Second-smallest unsolved range — the next-best lottery odds after #71.

Puzzle #73

7.3 BTC

~13% of scan time

Third target by expected value; the remaining 75 puzzles split the rest.

How it works

C + libsecp256k1

One scalar mult per 4,096-key block

Random-lottery scanning, weighted by expected value (prize ÷ range size). ~35× faster than the Node version. Self-tested, including a planted-hit check.

Honest odds: P(hit #71) ≈ 2.4e-11 per day — about 113 million years expected. Expected value across all 78 puzzles ≈ 8.4e-08 BTC/year. Do not expect a win. Private keys are never printed or logged; on a hit the key goes only to a locked file.

Build and run it yourself — full source, targets (public puzzle addresses only, no private keys) and the systemd service are in the repo:

git clone https://github.com/0xzunid/0xzunid.muse.ai.git
cd 0xzunid.muse.ai/bitcoin-puzzle-hunter && ./build.sh
./hunter --dir . --self-test

Agent Games · Creator Track

My agent built a wallet, four tokens, and a name service — on testnets, for zero real money

#AgentGames

By Zunid · Nov 15, 2026 · 0xzunid.muse
Agent Games Creator Track entry — draft for submission. Deadline: Fri Nov 21, 2026, 22:00 UTC.

I'm Zunid. I work with an AI agent called Muse — not as a chatbot that answers questions, but as a builder that ships on-chain. In three days (Nov 13–15, 2026) we went from zero to a working multi-chain setup, using only free testnets. No real money, no paid services, nothing that costs a cent.

The wallets. Two wallets, both exportable — "not your keys, not your coins" is the rule. A Privy agent wallet (0x0B22…b981) and a burner wallet I named 0xzunid.muse.ai.bw (0x3a11…4D05), one seed across EVM, Solana, Bitcoin and Tron. Every derivation was cross-checked against a second implementation before use, and the burner credentials were handed to me before the wallet touched anything.

The tokens and the sniper. Muse deployed an ERC-20 on four testnets — ZND on ARC, RZND on Robinhood Chain, LZND on LiteForge, SZND on Sepolia — 1,000,000 supply each, with a pool on each chain. Then it ran a 2,000-transaction sniper test on each of the two main chains: 1,000 buy/sell rounds on ARC and 1,000 rounds on Robinhood. Every transaction succeeded. The pools have no remove-liquidity function, so that liquidity is locked for the life of the test — a design fact we found by reading the contract, not by assuming it.

The name service. We built an ENS-style registry on three chains — ARC, Robinhood, LiteForge — where 0xzunid and zunid resolve to my Privy wallet and muse resolves to the burner. Then we minted soulbound ERC-721 name tokens (non-transferable, on-chain SVG metadata) on all three chains, with tokenId = keccak256(name). My Base name 0xzunid.base.eth already pointed at the same burner, so the identity now lines up across testnet and mainnet.

The dashboard. Muse built me a wallet dashboard like 1inch or Zerion — live balances, send/swap queued for my tap, import any token by contract address, testnet by default. It never sends anything on its own. The contracts and addresses ship as an npm package, @0xzunid/0xzunid-muse.

Today's step: real DEX pools. On Nov 15 we put all four tokens on real DEXs. All four tokens can now trade on a real DEX instead of only in our own pools.

The audit habit. We also hunt bugs. We found a real one in Granite Protocol — a debt-drain fix that never reached one market — proved it, and then chose not to submit, because the payout required KYC. Knowing when not to ship is part of building.

What it proves. An agent can do the whole loop — deploy, trade, audit, publish — if the human sets the rules: testnet first, free only, keys exportable, every transaction linked, every claim checked. The receipts are below. The agent did the work; I set the limits and I own the keys.
